I have one rule for feedback, and everything else follows from it. If the person cannot do something with it the next morning, it is not feedback yet. It is just an opinion I have made them carry. Be more strategic is not feedback. Cut the first three slides and open with the revenue line is feedback. So before I open my mouth I ask myself what exactly I want them to do differently, and if I cannot answer that in one sentence, I have not thought about it enough yet. Two other habits. I do not use the sandwich, the praise, then the criticism, then more praise. In the sandwich the praise exists only to cushion, everyone knows it, and people walk out remembering the two nice parts and nothing from the middle. I do praise, but separately and for something specific, because naming a behaviour is what reinforces it. And I name the behaviour, never the person. The opening lost the room is something we can fix together. You are not a strong presenter is something they have to defend themselves against, and once they are defending, they have stopped listening. When somebody goes defensive anyway, and it happens, I stop. I acknowledge the effort out loud, and then I ask a question instead of repeating the verdict.

In fifteen years I have been given a great deal of feedback and almost none of it changed anything. The kind that did nothing was always kind and always general. Be more strategic. Have more presence. I would nod, thank the person, and go back to my desk with no idea what to do on Monday morning. Then, four years ago, a director told me something very specific. She said that in meetings I answer questions I have not been asked, and that the habit makes me sound uncertain, as if I am still arguing with somebody who has already agreed. Stop at the answer, she said. That was the whole thing. One behaviour, one change. I will be honest about how it felt. I was defensive in the room, I explained myself twice, and I did not sleep especially well that night. A week later I called it the most useful thing anyone had ever said to me about my work, and I still catch myself doing it and stop. So now I ask for it in that shape. At the end of every review I ask for one thing I should keep doing and one thing I should change, and I refuse to leave the room with a general well done.

First, you reinforce one specific thing that worked, naming the behaviour and not the person, because a general well done reinforces nothing. Then, you name the one shortcoming, once and clearly, softening the pressure with could or might be worth, and never softening the message itself. After that, you make it actionable: say exactly what you would change, so the person can act on it the next morning. Next, if they become defensive, you stop, you acknowledge their point out loud, and you ask a question instead of repeating the verdict. Finally, you say what you are not saying, so nothing is left for them to imagine on the way home.
